newsitem.title: UK: UK grain trade say farmers sell, co-ops deny chang.
newsitem.headline: UK grain trade say farmers sell, co-ops deny chang.

text.p: UK grain traders reported signs of producer selling on Tuesday after a long period in which producers' unwillingness to come to market has underpinned weak prices. But co-operative managers said there was no rush to the market.
And traders' ideas were mixed on whether the latest sales could herald a shift in farmer behaviour.
"We've seen quite significant selling from co-operatives for the first time today," one said. "There are a few farmers cracking," another said.
But another reckoned farmers were still holding back. "They're driving themselves demented, but we don't think they're cracking yet," he said.

He reckoned 27-30 pct of the UK crop still had to be sold. "As time goes on so the window of opportunity disappears," he said. "If farmers don't take this market, then they are going to be getting something worse in the future."

"They are hoping that something will crop up," he said. He accused farmers of a lack of sophistication in dealing with the market. "They have little idea of what makes the market move," he said. "It's hardly been a difficult market to read."
"They've wanted yesterday's price all season and the man who's bitten the bullet and sold has been happy about it the day after, he said.
There had been farmer selling in recent days, he said, but not enough to look like a new trend.

Traders cited the continued weak tone in the UK market as the reason why farmers should sell. According to one, export shipments in January will come to no more than 200,000 tonnes. The market had been looking for 400,000 tonnes, he said. "There's going to be a lot of grain rolled forward into February," he said.

Sterling's strength has demolished UK competitiveness on other European markets, traders said. On Dec 3 the low on May futures was 95 stg and sterling was worth 8.64 against the French franc, one said.
At current sterling rates the future should be at 89.50 sterling, he said. It is actually at 92.65 stg. "So that's three quid's (pound's) worth of competitivity we've lost, he said.
Other felt the UK would struggle to export its surplus.

Co-operative managers felt more comfortable about the market. "We haven't been selling anything," the managing director of one east Anglian co-operative said. He explained that their grain was 70 per cent sold ahead for the season. "We're happy sitting on our hands for the other 30 per cent," he said.

"We haven't changed our policy. Certainly not today," another co-operative manager, based in southern England, said. "We've been steady sellers," he said. But he regretted not having sold more when prices were higher.

"If somebody had been holding back in the hope of an upsurge in exports and higher prices, maybe they would have to start doing something now," he said. "That would be a very contrary way of behaving in a commodity market," he said.
